items.title: An identical retry is accepted without a new row
items.body:
**Key: it returns the accepted indexes and leaves the chunk rows unchanged.**

The existing row's checksum equals the request's, so the conflict check passes. Storage commits, and the handler reaches `if (existing is null)`; the row exists, so no Add and no SaveChangesAsync happen. It then returns the ordered list of accepted indexes. That is idempotency as the concepts guide defines it: a retry preserves the accepted result.

Why the others are wrong:
- **409 because the index exists**: the 409 is only for a different checksum.
- **A second row**: the existing-row guard prevents it, and the unique index on (UploadSessionId, Index) would reject it anyway.
- **400 after a re-hash**: Committed is true, so the 400 branch is not reached.

excerpts.quote: if (existing is null)

items.title: Blobs are content-addressed and shared across users
items.body:
**Key: it reuses the existing blob row and adds a reference.**

The handler looks up a blob by ContentHash only, with no owner filter. For byte-identical content the hash matches, so it calls blob.AddReference(), which increments RefCount, and skips blobs.SaveAsync. A new blob is written only when no row has that hash.

Why the others are wrong:
- **A second copy**: the content-addressed lookup prevents it.
- **Overwrite**: the existing blob is never rewritten.
- **Rejected as a duplicate**: different users may hold the same content; each gets its own file node and version pointing at the shared blob.

excerpts.quote: blob.AddReference();

items.title: How a failed validator becomes a 400
items.body:
The start-upload action sends its command through MediatR, and Program.cs registers `ValidationBehavior` as a pipeline behavior that runs every validator for the request before the handler. When a rule fails, the behavior does not let FluentValidation's own exception escape. It joins the messages and throws an `AppException`, whose status defaults to `BadRequest`. The exception middleware maps an AppException to the status it carries, so the client gets a 400 whose title and detail are the rule's message.

Note what this depends on: the translation lives in the behavior. Had it thrown `ValidationException`, the middleware would have treated it as unexpected and answered 500.

- The handler never runs, so nothing is created.
- There is no 422 in this code base.
- The 500 arm is reached only by exception types the middleware does not name.

excerpts.quote: throw new AppException(string.Join("; ", failures.Select(x => x.ErrorMessage)));
HttpStatusCode statusCode = HttpStatusCode.BadRequest

items.title: Core idea: validate everything, then change state once
items.body:
Completing an upload turns accepted chunks into a stored file. CompleteUploadHandler does many things, and the order matters. List every step in the order it appears, and mark each one as a read-only check, an external write (blob storage or the queue), or a change to tracked database entities. Find the single SaveChangesAsync and note what comes after it.

Then read the first paragraph of 02-CONCEPTS.md and ask what a SHA-256 digest proves about an upload and what it cannot prove; check how the handler uses the value Hashing.Sha256WithLengthAsync returns. Read UserStorageAccount next: compare EnsureCanReserve, Reserve and Release, and note which ones change state and what each does at the edges. Last, read the paragraph on atomicity and name, for each step after the save, which resource would be left inconsistent if it failed.

excerpts.quote: Atomicity must always name its resource.

readMore.why: The completion handler, from index check to enqueue.

items.title: Not every absence is a 404
items.body:
ExceptionMiddleware has a concrete mapping: AppException to its own status, DomainException to 400, UnauthorizedAccessException to 401, and everything else to a 500 whose detail is hidden. An explicit not-found AppException can carry 404. But the upload Status action uses SingleAsync, and when no row matches, SingleAsync throws InvalidOperationException. That exception is none of the three mapped types, so it falls into the generic branch and the client sees a 500. Chapter 14 says to follow the actual branch rather than renaming every absence as a 404.

- SingleAsync throws on no rows; it does not return null.
- There is no blanket EF-to-409 rule.
- DomainException maps to 400, and it is not what a missing row raises.

excerpts.quote: Do not rename every absence as HTTP 404 without following the actual branch.

items.title: Returning a File result is not delivering the file
items.body:
A download action opens a stream and returns a File result with range processing. Its successful return does not mean the client received every byte: result execution, stream reads, network transport and client cancellation all happen afterwards. A service test can prove which stream was opened, not that delivery completed. The middleware also lacks a Response.HasStarted guard, and the AccessCount increment cannot tell a full transfer from a partial one.

- Authorization is configured on the controllers and host; File results do not skip it.
- The service did hand back a stream; the return shows that much, and nothing wraps a null.
- Scan checks happen in the service before the stream is returned.

excerpts.quote: The action's successful return does not mean the client has received all bytes.

items.title: Three size bounds, three different layers
items.body:
A chunk meets three separate limits. The chunk action declares a 64 MB request-size limit at the transport layer. StartUploadValidator allows a smaller configured range of chunk sizes for a session. And the filesystem adapter enforces the exact expected size for that particular index. A body can be under the transport ceiling yet too large for its index, and a final remainder chunk can be much smaller than the chunk size, so a test matrix needs each boundary.

- The user's quota is checked on other paths, not as a chunk-size bound.
- The session's TotalSize feeds the exact-size rule but is not itself one of the three.
- No blob-store maximum is involved.

excerpts.quote: These are three separate bounds: transport body ceiling, accepted session configuration, and exact chunk content length.

items.title: What an EF InMemory handler test can prove
items.body:
UploadHandlerTests run the real application handlers with fake chunk, blob and queue ports, then reopen the same named InMemory database to inspect usage, versions, blobs, jobs and session state. That proves the handler saved the expected graph in the fixture. It does not prove relational uniqueness, SQL rollback or behavior under competing database writers. InMemory does not even enforce the SQL unique index, so seeding the same chunk twice breaks the fixture, not the app.

- Unique indexes are not enforced by InMemory.
- No SQL transaction rollback is exercised.
- Two contexts on one in-memory store do not model real concurrent writers.

excerpts.quote: it does not prove relational uniqueness, SQL rollback, or competing database writers.

items.title: The last chunk is the remainder
items.body:
**Key: three chunks, and index 2 must hold exactly 2 bytes.**

Create computes ((totalSize - 1) / chunkSize) + 1 = ((10 - 1) / 4) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. ExpectedChunkSize(2) computes the offset 2 * 4 = 8 and returns Math.Min(4, 10 - 8) = 2. The handler passes that expected size to storage, and a chunk of any other length is not committed.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Two chunks with 6 bytes last**: chunks never exceed ChunkSize, so ten bytes need three.
- **Every chunk 4 bytes**: that would be 12 bytes, more than declared.
- **Any size up to 4**: the expected size is an exact length, not a maximum.

excerpts.quote: return Math.Min(ChunkSize, TotalSize - offset);

items.title: A pre-save name check is not a uniqueness invariant
items.body:
CreateFolderAsync asks whether a nondeleted sibling with the same owner, parent and name exists, then saves. Chapter 09 shows two reasons that is not a guarantee. The index over owner, parent, name and deleted flag is not declared unique, so two competing requests can both pass the check. And RenameAsync never runs the sibling query at all, so a rename can produce a duplicate that create would have refused.

- The check runs before the save, not after.
- The query includes the owner; collisions across users are not the issue.
- No root-folder exception is described.

excerpts.quote: It does not perform the create method's sibling-name existence query.

items.title: Trash is a flag on one node
items.body:
DeleteAsync marks the node deleted and saves. It does not recurse into descendants, remove blob bytes or release quota. RestoreAsync clears the flag and also skips any check for a new sibling that took the name meanwhile. Chapter 09 therefore calls trash a node-level state change, and says the meaning for a trashed folder's children has to be decided by reading the list, download, sharing and cleanup paths together.

- Descendants are not individually marked deleted by this method.
- Blob bytes stay where they are.
- There is no hidden trash folder; it is a flag on the row.

excerpts.quote: It does not recursively delete descendants in this method, remove blob bytes, or release quota.

items.title: Moving a folder under its own child
items.body:
MoveAsync checks that the destination parent belongs to the same owner and is a Folder. It never walks the descendants of the node being moved. FileNode.Move has a self-containment guard, but only when the node is a File. With root containing A and A containing B, moving A under B passes every check and creates the cycle A to B to A. A later traversal that assumes the tree is acyclic could loop or miss nodes.

- The domain guard does not run for folders.
- No ancestor walk exists in MoveAsync.
- B is an owned folder, so the ownership and type check passes.

excerpts.quote: FileNode.Move contains a self-containment guard only when the node is a File.

items.title: Someone else's session simply does not exist for you
items.body:
**Key: 404 "Upload session not found.", as the lookup is owner-scoped.**

UploadChunkHandler loads the session with `x.Id == request.SessionId && x.OwnerId == request.UserId`. For user B the query returns null and the ?? throws AppException("Upload session not found.", NotFound). The response is the same as for an id that does not exist, so B learns nothing about A's session.

Why the others are wrong:
- **403**: the code never separates exists-but-not-yours from missing.
- **Stored under A's session**: the owner filter stops that before any storage call.
- **409 not open**: the open-and-not-expired check runs only after a session is found.

excerpts.quote: x.Id == request.SessionId && x.OwnerId == request.UserId

items.title: Copy trusts whatever destination it is given
items.body:
Chapter 09 asks you to read each file operation on its own, and copy shows why. `MoveAsync` loads the destination through `GetOwnedNode`, so a folder that belongs to someone else, or does not exist, is refused before anything changes. `CopyAsync` has no such step. It loads the source file under the caller's owner id, adds a blob reference, builds the new node with the supplied `parentId` as it is, and saves.

The result is a node owned by the caller whose parent is another user's folder. It hangs under no folder of the caller's own tree, and the other user never lists it, because listings filter by owner and parent together. The same method also loads its source without a deleted filter, so a file sitting in the trash can be copied too.

- The owned-node lookup exists, but only move and the other node operations call it.
- The domain constructor checks names, not parents.
- No parent foreign key is configured in the model.

excerpts.quote: var copy = FileNode.CreateFile(userId, parentId, newName ?? $"Copy of {node.Name}");
It does not validate that destination parent with MoveAsync's helper in this method.

items.title: Searchable does not mean downloadable
items.body:
The search predicate matches on name or extracted text, scoped to the owner and excluding deleted nodes, but it has no scan-status gate like owner download has. Extracted text can stay on a node through a version change, so a phrase from the old version can still match while the new version waits for processing. Meanwhile the download path can refuse the file. Chapter 16 says both outcomes can hold at once without any inconsistency in the inspected branches.

- Pending nodes are not filtered out of search.
- The download gate refuses; it does not fall back to older bytes.
- AddVersion never clears the old text: it only adds the version and marks the node pending.

excerpts.quote: The search predicate does not include the same scan-status gate used by owner download.

items.title: Start here: a chunked upload, from session to saved file
items.body:
NetDropbox is a Dropbox-style file service in ASP.NET Core with EF Core. A client uploads a large file in pieces: it opens an upload session that declares the file's size, final SHA-256 digest and chunk size, sends each chunk by index, and then asks the server to complete the upload. This pack follows the **astraupskill/** course about making that path safe:

1. **01-CODEBASE-MAP.md**: who owns which rule, with a line map.
2. **02-CONCEPTS.md**: integrity, immutable chunks, quota preflight and atomicity.
3. **03-WORKED-CHANGE.md**: the before/after of the change, file by file.

One caution before you start. The filesystem storage adapter the course describes is not committed to git (the README's status note explains this), so its excerpt cannot be checked. Every quiz in this pack is answerable from committed files: UploadSession, UserStorageAccount, the two upload handlers and ExceptionMiddleware.

excerpts.quote: `src/NetDropbox.Infrastructure/Storage/FileSystemChunkStorage.cs` is **not in git**.

readMore.why: The course route and the status note about the missing storage file.
The line map: every rule with its owner and exact lines.

items.title: A matching digest does not prove the declared size
items.body:
**Key: a 400 for the size mismatch, raised before blob storage is reached.**

Hashing.Sha256WithLengthAsync returns a HashedContent with both Checksum and Length. The handler compares Length with session.TotalSize first and throws "Final file size does not match the upload session." (BadRequest), then compares the digest. The blob lookup and blobs.SaveAsync come after both checks, so nothing external is written. Quota is charged from TotalSize, which is why a truthful size matters.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Succeeds because the digest matches**: the length check fails first; a digest and a length answer different questions.
- **Checksum mismatch after saving**: the digest matches, and the failure happens before the blob step.
- **Succeeds charging 4 bytes**: that is the accounting hole the length check closes.

excerpts.quote: throw new AppException("Final file size does not match the upload session.", System.Net.HttpStatusCode.BadRequest);

items.title: Not committed: the handler says whether size or checksum failed
items.body:
**Key: a 400 saying the chunk size does not match the session boundary.**

When storage returns Committed = false, the handler chooses the message by comparing stored.Size with session.ExpectedChunkSize(request.Index). A different size gives "Chunk size does not match the session boundary."; an equal size means the checksum was the problem. Either way it throws AppException with BadRequest, which ExceptionMiddleware turns into 400.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The checksum message**: that branch applies only when the sizes match.
- **409**: conflicts are for an accepted index with different content.
- **413**: no handler or middleware produces that status.

excerpts.quote: "Chunk size does not match the session boundary."

items.title: Completion needs the exact index set first
items.body:
**Key: a 409 "Upload is missing chunks." before anything is assembled.**

CompleteUploadHandler reads the session's chunk indexes in order and requires both `chunkIndexes.Length == TotalChunks` and SequenceEqual with Enumerable.Range(0, TotalChunks). Indexes {0, 2} fail, so it throws AppException with Conflict. The quota preflight and OpenAssembledAsync come after this check.

Why the others are wrong:
- **400 for a short file**: the length comparison is never reached.
- **Saved without index 1**: the exact-set check exists to prevent that.
- **Waits for the chunk**: the handler does not wait; it fails immediately.

excerpts.quote: throw new AppException("Upload is missing chunks.", System.Net.HttpStatusCode.Conflict);

items.title: Different bytes at an accepted index: 409 up front
items.body:
**Key: a 409, raised before IChunkStorage is even called.**

The handler loads the existing UploadChunk for the session and index. When it exists and its checksum differs from the request's (compared ignoring case), it throws AppException("An accepted chunk cannot be replaced with different content.", Conflict). StoreAsync comes later, so storage never sees the new bytes.

Why the others are wrong:
- **200 and replaced**: accepted chunks are immutable; the concepts guide calls different content a conflict.
- **400 after storing**: the check happens before storage, and the status is 409.
- **200 keeping the old checksum**: the request is refused; nothing returns 200.

excerpts.quote: throw new AppException("An accepted chunk cannot be replaced with different content.", System.Net.HttpStatusCode.Conflict);

items.title: Core idea: a session declares the bytes, each chunk must fit them
items.body:
An upload session is a contract written before any bytes arrive. UploadSession.Create validates the declaration and works out how many chunks to expect; ExpectedChunkSize says how long each index must be. Work both out by hand for a few declarations: a size that divides evenly, one that does not, and a size of zero. Then compare the chunk-count arithmetic with what the worked change says it replaced, and ask why floating point was a poor tool there.

Next read UploadChunkHandler top to bottom and number its checks. For each check note what it compares, which exception it throws and with which HttpStatusCode. Pay attention to which checks run before the storage call and which after, and to what the handler does with the database row once storage has answered. Finally open ExceptionMiddleware and write down how each exception type becomes a status.

excerpts.quote: Its ExpectedChunkSize method defines the byte boundary for an index.

readMore.why: The session declaration, chunk arithmetic and lifecycle.
The chunk handler: lookup, checks, storage call and row write.

items.title: An empty file is one empty chunk
items.body:
**Key: one chunk, whose expected size is 0 bytes.**

Create special-cases zero: `totalSize == 0 ? 1 : ((totalSize - 1) / chunkSize) + 1`, so an empty file still needs one chunk. ExpectedChunkSize returns 0 when TotalSize is 0. The codebase map lists it as a rule: zero bytes = 1 chunk.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Zero chunks**: completion requires the index set 0..TotalChunks-1, and TotalChunks is 1.
- **Create throws**: only a negative size is rejected.
- **A full padded chunk**: nothing pads; the expected size is 0.

excerpts.quote: var requiredChunks = totalSize == 0 ? 1 : ((totalSize - 1) / chunkSize) + 1;

items.title: Integer ceiling, then an explicit int guard
items.body:
**Key: integer ceiling division, then a check that the count fits an int.**

The new code computes the count in long arithmetic as ((totalSize - 1) / chunkSize) + 1, which rounds up exactly, then throws DomainException("Upload requires too many chunks.") when it exceeds int.MaxValue, and only then casts to int. The old version went through double and an unchecked cast, which can lose precision and, for huge counts, wrap.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Decimal division**: no decimal type is used.
- **Math.Ceiling then an unchecked cast**: that is close to the old behavior the change removed.
- **A checked block**: the guard is an explicit comparison, not checked arithmetic.

excerpts.quote: if (requiredChunks > int.MaxValue) throw new DomainException("Upload requires too many chunks.");

items.title: Offsets point into a set that keeps changing
items.body:
Search orders by name and pages with Skip and Take. Page one returns Atlas and Birch. If Aardvark is inserted before the next request, the set becomes Aardvark, Atlas, Birch, Cedar, Delta, and offset two now starts at Birch, so Birch appears twice. A deletion causes the opposite, a skipped row. Neither needs a broken database; offsets describe positions in the current set, not in the earlier snapshot.

- No snapshot of page one is held between requests.
- New rows sort by name, so Aardvark comes first, not last.
- Inserts do not invalidate anything; the next query simply sees them.

excerpts.quote: Offset pagination describes positions in the current ordered set

items.title: Checked one way, stored another
items.body:
The domain cleans folder names by trimming them. But CreateFolderAsync runs its existence query with the raw name from the request, before the folder is constructed. A name with surrounding spaces is therefore checked as " Reports " and stored as "Reports", so the check and the stored value can disagree. Provider collation may also change how case compares. Chapter 09's conclusion: normalization and comparison must be specified at the authoritative boundary.

- The query does not trim; the domain does, later.
- The chapter does not describe lowercasing.
- Spaces around a name are cleaned, not rejected.

excerpts.quote: The result can differ from the name used in the existence query.

items.title: Quota is checked read-only, before any expensive work
items.body:
**Key: 400 from a DomainException, decided before assembly starts.**

After the index check, the handler loads the user and calls user.EnsureCanReserve(session.TotalSize). EnsureCanReserve compares against the remaining capacity by subtraction and throws DomainException("Storage quota exceeded.") without changing state. ExceptionMiddleware maps DomainException to 400. OpenAssembledAsync, hashing and the blob write all come later.

Why the others are wrong:
- **413**: nothing maps quota to Payload Too Large.
- **409 after the blob write**: the worked change moved quota before the blob write precisely to avoid that.
- **507 via AppException**: the quota check throws DomainException, not AppException, and no code uses 507.

excerpts.quote: throw new DomainException("Storage quota exceeded.");
DomainException => StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest,

items.title: Work after the save is outside its transaction
items.body:
**Key: the file version and scan job are saved, yet the scan message is lost.**

Line 85 commits one EF unit of work: blob reference, file node, version, ProcessingJob, quota reservation and the completed session. Chunk deletion and EnqueueAsync run afterwards. If the enqueue throws, the committed rows stay, the queued message never exists, and the request fails with a 500 from the middleware. The concepts guide says neither boundary makes the blob write and queue call part of one global transaction.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Everything rolls back**: the transaction already committed; the queue is an in-memory channel outside it.
- **The blob is deleted**: the code deliberately avoids deleting a content-addressed blob after an uncertain failure.
- **Retried in-process**: there is no retry loop around the enqueue.

excerpts.quote: await queue.EnqueueAsync(new ProcessingMessage(file.Id, version.Id, scanJob.Id), cancellationToken);

items.title: Beyond uploads: folders, HTTP layers, storage, search and logs
items.body:
The newer questions leave the upload path and draw on five chapters of `astraupskill/extended-course/` plus the course's testing page.

Chapter 09 traces the file operations (create, rename, move, copy, delete, restore) one by one. Chapter 14 follows a request through controllers, validators, handlers and the exception middleware. Chapter 15 compares the local and object-storage blob adapters. Chapter 16 treats search as a read model that changes between requests. Chapter 17 designs diagnostic evidence around the system's real boundaries. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` asks what each kind of test can and cannot prove.

These chapters are careful about evidence: they separate what the source shows from what would need a hosted run or a real database. Read each claim with that distinction in mind.

excerpts.quote: A direct handler call is not the same execution path as an authenticated HTTP request.
File operations often share a service but enforce different preconditions.

items.title: Release never takes usage below zero
items.body:
**Key: 0, since Release clamps the result at zero.**

Release throws only when bytes is negative. Otherwise it sets UsedBytes = Math.Max(0, UsedBytes - bytes): 3 - 5 is -2, and Math.Max(0, -2) is 0.

Why the others are wrong:
- **-2**: the Math.Max call is the lower bound.
- **3, ignored**: the subtraction still happens, it is just clamped.
- **A DomainException**: releasing more than is used is not an error here; only negative input throws.

excerpts.quote: UsedBytes = Math.Max(0, UsedBytes - bytes);

items.title: A direct handler call skips the validation pipeline
items.body:
A real request routes and binds, the controller derives the user, and MediatR's ValidationBehavior runs the registered validators before the handler. Calling StartUploadHandler.Handle directly skips binding and that pipeline. The domain constructor can still reject some values, but the validator's chunk-size interval never runs, so a test that succeeds with a tiny chunk size says nothing about what the public API accepts.

- Validators run in the pipeline, not inside the handler.
- The 64 MB request limit is a separate transport bound.
- Authorization middleware also does not run in a direct call.

excerpts.quote: Calling StartUploadHandler.Handle directly bypasses controller binding and the MediatR pipeline.

items.title: Copying content also copies assumptions
items.body:
CopyAsync adds a version that points to the same blob, then marks the copy clean using the source node's extracted text and thumbnail. It does not run the scanner, and it does not look at the source's ScanStatus before calling MarkScanClean. Chapter 09 flags the risk: if the source is pending, failed or infected, a clean copy could contradict the download policy. A safer contract would require verified clean evidence for the exact version copied.

- No new scan job is enqueued for the copy.
- The status is set to clean, not copied from the source.
- There is no source-is-clean condition in the method.

excerpts.quote: It also does not check source ScanStatus before calling MarkScanClean.
